title: Where Exactly Does the Tefach Go?
subtitle: Five different answers for positioning the minimal third wall, then whether a sukkah-wall for Shabbos is the same thing as a sukkah-wall for Sukkot.
sources: Gemara text: Sefaria (William Davidson Edition). Structure and quiz questions 1-2, 4 cross-checked against the Dafyomi Advancement Forum (dafyomi.co.il) quiz for Sukkah 7. Tosfos: dafyomi.co.il's "Point by Point Summary of Tosfos" (Yaakov Montrose, Kollel Iyun Hadaf).
before: 6b ended with Rav being asked where the token tefach-wide third wall actually gets positioned. This amud runs through five different answers to that one practical question — from silence, to "opposite the emerging wall," to an expanded "tefach sochek" near a corner, to requiring an actual doorway-shape (tzuras ha'petach).

Then it turns to a related but separate question: if that same tefach counts as a wall for sukkah, does it automatically count as a wall for carrying on Shabbos too — even though sukkah-law and Shabbos-law don't usually import rulings from each other so freely?

flow.label: Five positions for the sukkah made of two parallel walls ("like an alleyway")

items.label: Rav Kahana/Asi's suggestion
items.sub: opposite the diagonal — Rav stayed silent

items.label: Shmuel/Levi, and the study hall
items.sub: opposite the gap left by the emerging wall

items.label: Rabbi Simon / R' Yehoshua ben Levi
items.sub: an expanded tefach, within 3 tefachim of a wall (lavud)

items.label: Rava (three versions)
items.sub: needs a doorway-shape (tzuras ha'petach) — instead of, in addition to, or regardless of the expanded tefach

flow.label: A harder case: no standing walls at all touch each other
flow.sub: needs a real board, over 4 tefachim wide, not just an expanded tefach — the lavud trick alone isn't enough without real walls to anchor to

flow.label: New question: does a sukkah-qualifying tefach-wall also count for Shabbos carrying?

items.label: Rava
items.sub: yes — since it's a wall for sukkah, it's a wall for Shabbos too (miggo)

items.label: Abaye challenges
items.sub: a beraita implies Shabbos-during-Sukkot is actually stricter than sukkah generally, not more lenient

flow.label: Resolved: the beraita is comparing ordinary Shabbos to Sukkot-Shabbos, not sukkah-law to Shabbos-law
flow.sub: leniency-to-stringency is unremarkable; the reverse direction is what actually needed stating — continues onto 7b

flowCaption: A practical question given five different answers, then a separate question about borrowing rulings between sukkah-law and Shabbos-law.

opinions.who: Rabbi Simon (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi)
opinions.claim: An expanded tefach (measured with fingers spread), placed within 3 tefachim of a real wall, works via lavud to effectively become a 4-tefach wall.
opinions.basis: The lavud principle: anything closer than 3 tefachim to a wall is treated as joined to it.

opinions.claim: The two-parallel-walls sukkah is valid only with a doorway-shape (tzuras ha'petach) for the third side — reported in three different versions of exactly how this relates to the expanded-tefach option.
opinions.basis: A doorway-frame (two side-posts and a crossbeam) counts as a halachic partition in its own right.

script.speaker: First suggestion, unanswered
script.quote: וְיַעֲמִידֶנּוּ כְּנֶגֶד רֹאשׁ תּוֹר?! שְׁתֵיק רַב.
script.gloss: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi suggest positioning the tefach opposite the diagonal line where two walls would converge, like a triangle's third side. Rav had no response.

script.speaker: Shmuel/Levi, and the study hall
script.gloss: Position it opposite the gap left by the end of one of the standing walls — the standard ruling.

script.speaker: Rabbi Simon (or R' Yehoshua ben Levi)
script.quote: עוֹשֶׂה לוֹ טֶפַח שׂוֹחֵק, וּמַעֲמִידוֹ בְּפָחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה טְפָחִים סָמוּךְ לַדּוֹפֶן.
script.gloss: Make it an expanded tefach and position it within 3 tefachim of a real wall — lavud treats it as joined to that wall, effectively widening it.

script.speaker: Rav Yehuda adds
script.quote: סוּכָּה הָעֲשׂוּיָה כְּמָבוֹי — כְּשֵׁרָה, וְאוֹתוֹ טֶפַח מַעֲמִידוֹ לְכׇל רוּחַ שֶׁיִּרְצֶה.
script.gloss: A sukkah built like an alleyway (two parallel full walls) is fit, and that tefach can go on whichever side he wants — it's just a marker at that point.

script.speaker: The harder case
script.gloss: Where there aren't even two properly standard walls to begin with, an expanded tefach isn't enough — it takes a real board, just over 4 tefachim wide, positioned within 3 tefachim of a wall.

script.speaker: Gemara asks the obvious question
script.quote: וּמַאי שְׁנָא הָתָם דְּקָאָמְרַתְּ סַגִּיא טֶפַח שׂוֹחֵק, וּמַאי שְׁנָא הָכָא דְּקָאָמְרַתְּ בָּעֲיָא פַּס אַרְבָּעָה?
script.gloss: Why does the easier case only need an expanded tefach, but the harder case needs a full 4-tefach board?

script.speaker: Answered
script.gloss: Where two standard walls already exist, a small addition suffices. Where they don't, lavud alone can't manufacture a wall from nothing — it needs a real board to anchor to.

script.speaker: Rava adds a further requirement — three versions
script.gloss: (1) The two-wall sukkah is valid only with a doorway-shape (tzuras ha'petach) for the third side. (2) Some report: it's also valid this way — not rejecting the expanded-tefach option, just offering an alternative. (3) Others report: it also requires a doorway-shape, in addition to the expanded tefach — both together.

script.speaker: Practical footnote
script.gloss: Rav Ashi found Rav Kahana building both the expanded-tefach wall and a doorway-shape — confirming Rav Kahana held by the third, most stringent version of Rava's ruling.

script.speaker: New question
script.quote: וְכֵן לְשַׁבָּת, מִגּוֹ דְּהָוְיָא דּוֹפֶן לְעִנְיַן סוּכָּה — הָוְיָא דּוֹפֶן לְעִנְיַן שַׁבָּת.
script.gloss: Rava: since that tefach counts as a wall for sukkah purposes, it also counts as a partition for Shabbos carrying — on Shabbos that falls during Sukkot, at least.

script.speaker: Abaye objects
script.quote: וְהָתַנְיָא: דּוֹפֶן סוּכָּה כְּדוֹפֶן שַׁבָּת... וִיתֵירָה, שַׁבָּת עַל סוּכָּה.
script.gloss: But a beraita explicitly compares the two sets of laws and says Shabbos is more stringent than sukkah (Shabbos partitions need standing sections to outweigh gaps; sukkah doesn't) — implying they're kept separate, not automatically borrowed from each other!

script.speaker: Reread
script.quote: לָא: יְתֵירָה שַׁבָּת דְעָלְמָא עַל שַׁבָּת דְּסוּכָּה.
script.gloss: No — the beraita is comparing ordinary Shabbos to Shabbos-during-Sukkot specifically, not sukkah-law to Shabbos-law generally. On Sukkot's Shabbos, the miggo does apply.

script.speaker: One more push, continuing to 7b
script.gloss: If that's the real distinction, shouldn't the beraita also have spelled out the reverse — a case where sukkah-law is more lenient than its own Shabbos? Rava: no novelty is needed for leniency flowing into a stricter law (sukkah's ruling applying to Shabbos); the reverse would be the real chiddush, and that's covered elsewhere — continued on 7b.

tosfos.summary: Why the airspace on both sides of the tefach-wall doesn't nullify it, unlike similar cases elsewhere.

points.label: (a) Implied Question
points.he: אף על גב דאכיוצא בזה אמר פ' קמא דעירובין... אתי אוירא דהאי גיסא ודהאי גיסא ומבטל ליה
points.en: Elsewhere (Eruvin 10b), airspace on both sides of a narrow object is said to nullify it. Why not here?

points.label: (b) Answer
points.he: הכא דטפח מחיצה דאורייתא והלכתא גמירי לה לא אתי אוירא ומבטל לה
points.en: Here the tefach is a Torah-level wall by transmitted halachah — that status is strong enough that surrounding airspace doesn't nullify it.

tosfos.summary: Why Sukkah's doorway-shape requirement is stricter than the ordinary one used for Eruvin.

points.label: (a) Implied Question
points.he: בפ' קמא דעירובין לא יהבינן שיעורא לקנה של צורת פתח... אלא שתהא בריאה כדי לעמוד בה דלת
points.en: In Eruvin, a doorway-shape needs no minimum thickness for its posts — any width holds, as long as it could support a door. Why does Sukkah demand thicker posts?

points.label: (2) Answer
points.he: גבי סוכה החמירו דבעינן מחיצות הניכרות
points.en: Sukkah is held to a higher standard — it requires genuinely recognizable walls.

tosfos.summary: The Tannaim on Abaye's "dirat keva" list don't all apply the principle identically — they just share the underlying intuition.

points.label: (a)-(b) Not all the same
points.he: על כרחיך אין שוין דהא רבי בעי ד' אמות ולב"ש סגי בכדי ראשו ורובו ושולחנו
points.en: They clearly aren't identical positions — Rabbi requires a full 4×4 amos, while Beit Shammai settles for just "head, most of the body, and table." Each applies "sukkah must resemble a permanent dwelling" to a different degree.

tosfos.summary: Whether the beraita about Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Akiva's machloket even includes the case of a sukkah on a wagon.

points.label: (a) Text question
points.he: לקמן בפרק הישן במתני' דקתני כשרה גרסינן בראש העגלה אבל הכא בברייתא... אור"ת דלא גרסינן ליה
points.en: Rabbeinu Tam and Rabbeinu Chananel's texts omit "wagon" from this particular beraita — since the real machloket (per 23a) turns on withstanding an ordinary land-wind versus a sea-wind, which doesn't obviously apply to a wagon at all.

points.label: Left unresolved
points.he: ומיהו יש לדחות דכי האי גוונא אמר יכולה לעמוד ברוח מצויה דארץ ואינה יכולה לעמוד ברוח מצויה שבראש העגלה
points.en: Tosfos also considers the opposite: the same land/sea-wind distinction could be reframed for a wagon too — leaving the textual question genuinely open.
